paras: The lynching of John and Edward Lovelace was the shooting of a Black farmer and his son by a group of white men at their home in Woodbury, Georgia, in August 1910. According to the wire report, the men were killed to punish them for saying that a white man had stolen their corn. The dispatch ran in white papers from Mississippi and Louisiana to Ohio and Washington and in the Black weekly the Advocate, which headlined the white men as the accused robbers.

The Lovelaces were described as "prosperous farmers" at Woodbury. They were said to have circulated reports that corn had been stolen from them by a member of a prominent white family, named in most white copy as Oscar Parks.

On the afternoon of the killing, Parks, his four brothers and several other white men went to the Lovelaces' home "to punish them for circulating the reports." The whites seized the two men and demanded that they retract the charge. When they refused, and, "it is said," prepared to defend themselves, the white men opened fire and "riddled" them with bullets. Both fell dead almost at their doorstep.
No report of an arrest, inquest, grand jury action or trial appears in the coverage, and no Georgia paper's account was found.

The story reached print as a single wire dispatch, and every version traces to it. The Marion Daily Mirror in Ohio carried the earliest item found, on August 17, a one-line digest saying the two "colored" men were shot "by a mob." On August 18 and 19 the Oxford Eagle, the Port Gibson Reveille and the Macon Beacon in Mississippi and the Tensas Gazette in Louisiana printed the full text under "Two Negroes Shot to Death," with the subhead "Accused a White Man of Stealing Their Corn." The Perrysburg Journal in Ohio shortened it under "Father and Son Are Slain," ending with "The shooting followed," and the Spokane Press reduced it to a sentence on August 20.

The Advocate printed the same body text on August 18 but omitted Parks's name and changed the emphasis of the headline. Where white headlines led with the victims' accusation, the Advocate's read "White Men Accused of Robbing Two Georgia Negroes Shoot Them to Death." Neither press added editorial comment, and all versions told the story from the attackers' side, including the unsourced claim that the victims prepared to defend themselves.

The victims' surname appears as Lovelace in the Advocate and two Ohio papers and as Loveland in the Mississippi and Louisiana copy. The date is also uncertain: the Advocate's dateline reads "August 10" with the shooting "late this afternoon," while other copy places it "late Monday afternoon," and August 10, 1910, was a Wednesday.

reader.title: Lynching of John and Edward Lovelace
bases: A group of white men went to the Lovelaces' home to punish them for an accusation against a white man and shot them dead (A2, A3).

The wire reports that a white man, his four brothers and several other white men, with no stated legal authority, went to the house 'to punish' John and Edward Lovelace for saying corn had been stolen from them, and shot both dead when they refused to retract (A2, A3, A5). The killing was carried out as punishment for a Black family's charge against a white man, a pretext of race and tradition.
Every version, Black and white, is the same Woodbury wire dispatch or a condensation of it (A1, A2, A3, A5, A8); no local Georgia report, inquest or independent account was found.

accounts.label: Woodbury wire dispatch
accounts.gist: The Lovelaces, prosperous Black farmers, said a white man of a prominent family had stolen their corn; he, his four brothers and other whites went to their home to punish them, seized them, demanded a retraction, and when they refused and, 'it is said', prepared to defend themselves, shot them dead.

accounts.label: News digest
accounts.gist: A one-line summary saying the two men were shot to death 'by a mob' for accusing a white man of stealing corn.

framing.detail: Mississippi and Louisiana weeklies ran the dispatch under 'Two Negroes Shot to Death / Accused a White Man of Stealing Their Corn', making the victims' accusation the headline cause; the Marion daily mirror called the killers 'a mob'.
The Perrysburg journal headlined it 'Father and Son Are Slain' and cut the seizure, the demand to retract and the shooting details to 'The shooting followed.'

The Advocate ran the wire body unchanged but headlined it 'White Men Accused of Robbing Two Georgia Negroes Shoot Them to Death', making the white men the subject and the accused robbers; it added no comment.

conflicts.note: Wire variants; the Black-press copy and two white papers give Lovelace.
August 10, 1910 fell on a Wednesday, so the dateline and 'Monday' cannot both be right; the coverage does not settle which is correct.

Oscar Parks, his four brothers and several other white men, per the wire.
lynching: a group of five or more white men killed two Black men to punish them for an accusation against a white man.
Advocate dateline August 10, 1910; other wire copy says 'Monday' afternoon.
To 'punish them for circulating the reports' that a white man stole their corn; they refused to retract and, 'it is said', prepared to defend themselves.
Not in custody; seized at their own home.
No article names the county; only Woodbury, Ga.
